content.summary_of_the_paper:
This submission proposes an approach for object goal navigation task that forms a 3D point-based sparse map and uses this map to check spatial semantic consistency for navigation. The primary motivation for this approach is that previous works ignore that objects lie in the 3D world. Hence, using 3D representations from multi-view observations during navigation may acquire more accurate object recognition. 

The proposed method takes in RGB-D observations and the label of the target object to navigate in an unmapped scene.
The proposed approach incorporates online 3D semantic point fusion with two-stage policy learning. The 3D semantic point fusion module updates temporal semantic prediction and consistency, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the environments. The two-stage policy can be separated into exploration and verification. In the exploration stage, with the input of 3D points, the policy learns to predict a discrete direction in a low dimension. In the verification stage, the policy learns to adjust a confidence threshold to accommodate different categories dynamically.

The experiments are conducted on Gibson and Matterport3D. The improvements of the proposed method seem limited.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

+ The idea of combining 3D semantic points with object goal task is sensible and clear. Recognizing objects via 3D semantic points from multi-view observations during navigation seems  more interesting and reasonable than 2D semantic points.
- The paper develops a two-stage method to improve sample efficiency, which is important in 3D representation for reducing computational resources.
- The illustrations are vivid and easy to understand.

**Weaknesses:**

- The technical contribution seems unclear. There seem to be too many words about the previous works (e.g., 3D point fusion algorithm, heuristic goal selection) in the Approach part. In this case, I cannot clearly separate the improvements in this work or previous works. Besides, the technical improvement (e.g., max fusion) seems a little weak, and I worry that the contribution of these modifications is sufficient either in the method description or experimental evaluation.
- I noticed that the comparison baselines (e.g., PONI, SemExp) seem to perform worse than the results in their published papers. Is there any reason for this? Besides, the performance improvements are tiny (32.6 vs 31.8, 41.7 vs 41.0, 73.6 vs 72.5). I think the author should describe the proposed method’s advantages more clearly.
- The submission mentions that “2D semantic prediction already achieves impressive improvement”. Does this mean that 3D semantic points are not so necessary?
- Maybe there is a need to explain more about equation 2. I don’t actually get what this equation does in the task.
- I wonder if the $\tau_{low}$ is a hyper-parameter? Is there any reason or ablations to demonstrate why it is set to 0.75?
- Is it possible to explain the meaning of the “KL map” in Figure 5? The concept of the KL map seems to lack descriptions.
- What is the meaning of “3D points are naturally more memory-efficient.”

Some advice on typos:

- Line 30: “Hence if the agent” -> “Hence, if the agent”
- Line 94: “and novel verification stage” -> “and a novel verification stage”
- Line 215: “and , the” -> “and, the”
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The main idea of utilizing 3D semantic points with the object goal task is sensible and clear. Furthermore, I think this idea is novel for current ObjectNav methods. However, I think the technical contribution is unclear, and the improvements are limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I like the idea of recognizing objects in 3D view. The recognition may benefit from multi-view observations during navigation. However, I am concerned about the technical contribution, improvement, and unclear descriptions (see weakness for details). Therefore, I rate for borderline, but I'm looking forward to the author's reply.

content.title: Response to reviewer nL2X
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer nL2X for the kind and insightful comments. We answer some of your concerns below:

> 1. "What is the difference between the proposed method and previous works? The technical contribution of the method?"

Our major contribution lies in enabling a 3D-aware agent for ObjectNav by decomposing the navigation policy into two dedicated designed exploration and verification policies. Both two policies take 3D points as observation and output low-dimensional discrete actions. This enables our method to efficiently leverage the semantic scene understanding in fine-grained 3D space to explore the surrounding environment and verify the target object.

> 2. "I noticed that the comparison baselines (e.g., PONI, SemExp) seem to perform worse than the results in their published papers. Is there any reason for this?"

Some baselines (L2M, SemExp, Stubborn) didn't provide their results on the Matterport3D validation dataset. So we re-evaluate their performance based on their open-source code. And for PONI, we directly quote their result from their paper.

Moreover, we also conducted an experiment on the same dataset used by L2M, SemExp in their paper. We achieved 21.2 SPL compared to 17.0 SPL from L2M. See table.5 in suppl. A.4 for more details.

>3. "What is the meaning of *3D points are naturally more memory-efficient*."

The indoor scenes comprise many empty spaces, which is a significant waste to store in dense voxels. However, the points are only distributed along the scenes' surface, which leads to a more memory-efficient representation.

> 4. "The concept of sequence 2, KL map, and hyper-parameters is mislearning."

Thanks for pointing it out. We will carefully revise the manuscript to better explain our designs.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a 3D-aware two-stage object goal navigation approach.

An agent first conducts an exploration policy to determine a goal direction and then utilizes a local planner to navigate toward the predicted goal direction. During approaching the goal direction, the agent applies a verification module to decide whether the agent should stop.

SOTA performances are achieved on the Gibson and MP3D validation datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- Figures and tables are clearly presented.
- The proposed method achieves SOTA performance on SPL in both Gibson and MP3D validation datasets. 


Cons:
- The proposed method does not outperform other methods on Success Rate in both environments.
- Some claims cannot be well supported by model design and experiment results. For example, the paper claims that 3D structure mainly benefits the model by providing highly accurate semantic predictions. However, in applying 3D structure to 2D top-down map, the author includes an obstacle map besides semantic channels. Therefore, I have two questions about this obstacle map. First, what procedure is used to obtain this obstacle map? Second, what is the result of the proposed method without this obstacle map?
- Furthermore, I am curious about performance improvements brought by the 3D semantic prediction. Is it possible to provide the experiment that only removes the semantic channels in $C_{2D}$ and spatial semantic consistency/semantic channels in $C_{3D}$.
- Meanwhile, the proposed approach is a two-stage method. At the beginning, I understand it should be one stage after the other.  However, after reading the paper, it seems that both stages are running parallel. Could you please correct me if I understand wrongly?
- For the exploration stage, what if the agent predicts a wrong goal direction? Does the agent only predict one time and navigate to the goal direction regardless of the effectiveness of the predicted goal direction?  OR will it predict again? If it will predict again, what is the trigger for re-prediction?
- Different from previous methods, the paper explicitly utilizes depth to estimate a 3D sparse map. Therefore, suppose there is an error in depth maps, will it raise the misalignment of point fusion? I am interested in the corresponding impact on navigation performance.
- Additionally, the agent in [1] for the object goal navigation task could operate 6 different actions, while the agent in the paper only has 4 actions to be selected. Could the author please explain the difference and the performance impact between the two action spaces?


[1] Ramrakhya, R., Undersander, E., Batra, D., & Das, A. (2022). Habitat-Web: Learning Embodied Object-Search Strategies from Human Demonstrations at Scale. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 5173-5183).

content.title: Responce to reviewer 8MhK
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer 8MhK for the valuable comments and suggestions. 

>1. "What procedure is used to obtain this obstacle map? What is the result of the proposed method without this obstacle map?"

The obstacle map is obtained by following existing modular-based methods [1,2], which use a deterministic projection algorithm. And The obstacle map is necessary for our local planner to perform path planning. Though, alternatives exist, e.g., vision-based local planners. The research about the local panner is out of the scope of this work.


>2. "Performance improvements brought by the 3D semantic prediction."

In Table 3, we validate the improvement of using 3D semantic prediction (form 12.8 to 13.5 in SPL). And we also give a qualitative result (see Fig. 6) on various scenes where the 3D semantic prediction leads to more consistent results. 


>3. "Suppose there is an error in depth maps, will it raise the misalignment of point fusion?"

Yes, the errors of depth maps could lead to misalignment for modular-based ObjectNav methods, which use depth maps as inputs, including ours. Therefore, our method will remove the points that have relatively large distances (greater than 15cm, see suppl A.2) from the so far constructed scene. This strategy has been proven effective in dealing with real RGBD sequences in [3].


>4. "How the two-stage policy works?"

Your understanding is correct. The exploration policy and verification policy are running in parallel. We agree that the term "stage" is misleading and will be revised in the future submission.


>5. "Why only use four actions rather than all six actions in the habitat challenge."

The Habitat GoalNav simulator does provide six actions: *Move Forward*, *Turn Left*, *Turn Right*, *Stop*, *Look Up* and *Look Down*, but we leave out the last two camera-pitch actions in our setting, as did in the majority of other modular-based works in the filed[1,2]. We found that the *Look Up* and *Look Down* actions offer limited new observations (mostly cell and floor), which damage the efficiency of navigation. 
We do agree that these two pitch-camera actions could play a crucial part in finding table-top objects, e.g., bottles and cups. This could be a following work of our method.

[1] Ramakrishnan S K, Chaplot D S, Al-Halah Z, et al. PONI: Potential Functions for ObjectGoal Navigation with Interaction-free Learning[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022: 18890-18900.

[2] McCormac J, Handa A, Davison A, et al. Semanticfusion: Dense 3d semantic mapping with convolutional neural networks[C]//2017 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and automation (ICRA). IEEE, 2017: 4628-4635.

[3] Georgakis G, Bucher B, Schmeckpeper K, et al. Learning to Map for Active Semantic Goal Navigation[C]//International Conference on Learning Representations. 2021.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The manuscript considers the object nav goal task in Embodied AI.

The proposed approach combines what it calls "online semantic point fusion" (using a 3D sparse map — defined by prior art — to retrieve points within a neighborhood of a query point, in which 3D object structures may manifest) with a "two-stage RL approach for exploration and verification" (frontier-based exploration + iterative comparison of the 3D sparse map representation with the target category ID).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
(Strengths)

The proposed approach considers a compelling problem in Embodied AI.

The proposed approach is predicated on strong principles of modularity and decomposition of objectives, with the goal of enabling sample-efficiency and generalization.

(Weaknesses)

Section 2: "GoalNav with Visual Sequences.": For each paragraph, the manuscript should not forget to state what the proposed method does differently.

Section 3: What if a target goal along a specific direction is never verified? Does the agent just move forward forever, until the maximum number of actions is executed and the episode ends?

Section 3.3: "Exploration Stage", Verification Stage: Discussion comparing the proposed approach with the related work should have been provided earlier — in the Related Works section. This section should focus exclusively on the describing the methodology, since it should have been appropriately and logically justified. The fact that further justification is necessary confirms the notion that logical premises, clear hypotheses, and grounded research questions are largely absent from the earlier part of the manuscript.

Section 3.3: The manuscript defines an exploration policy that "predicts a goal direction dt ∈ D that drives the agent to find the target category object as soon as possible", but does not later justify/explain what mechanism is responsible for enabling the agent to find the category object expeditiously. It is not sufficient or appropriate for the manuscript to simply state this as an intention or attribute of the approach, without justification. Through the reward structure only, which is agnostic of the policy, the agent is encouraged to embark on unexplored areas — which may or may not contain the category object.

Section 3.3: Missing intuition — where does the \tau_{\text{low}} value of 0.75 come from? Where does (3) come from?

Section 4: The main results are unconvincing. For both Gibson and MP3D, the proposed approach does not yield compelling SR values. The likely reason that SPL is competitive is that path lengths are relatively short — one aspect in favor of the proposed approach. Despite this, however, Gibson-val SPL is within 7-tenths of a percentage point of the next best-scoring approach. I would love to see averaged results over multiple runs, with standard deviation information.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity/quality: The clarity in this manuscript is very low: the manuscript is replete with run-on sentences, sentence fragments, lack of punctuation, and a tendency to obfuscate meaning with excessive jargon. Certain parts of the manuscript are virtually unreadable.

Clarity/quality: The manuscript makes little attempt break down complex concepts into more palatable components.

Clarity/quality: The introduction of concepts and ideas in the manuscript do not follow a consistent logical flow. The manuscript contains several instances where a methodological description is accompanied with hasty justifications. An example: "When the agent observes something that is predicted with goal semantic label and needs to decide whether marches to the place [sic], our proposed verification policy learns to dynamically adjust a confidence threshold to accommodate different object categories, and we can further use the spatial semantic consistency to check whether we can trust the semantic prediction, which makes our navigation robust to semantic errors." It would have been better if the manuscript began with clearly articulated hypotheses and followed up with reasonable conclusions, supported by empirical or theoretical analysis.

Clarity/quality: Terms such as "naturally", "proved", and "multi-view" are misused.

Clarity/quality: The manuscript contains several instances of improper citation formats — i.e., "\citet" where "\citep" should be used.

Clarity/quality: The manuscript has an inconsistent paragraph structure, with stray sentences separated from the surround text.

Novelty: All components in the proposed work were borrowed directly from existing works; little additional insight was provided, beyond a discussion of the engineering involved.

Reproducibility: Whereas the manuscript provides a high-level template for each module's underlying components (mostly by specifying the preexisting work that each component was borrowed from), specific details are lacking from the main content of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Low clarity

Missing hypotheses and justifications

Unconvincing experimental results

Unsupported claims
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: Response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their valuable comments and constructive suggestions. 

We are excited to report that our method has been drastically improved with significant performance improvement during the past few months. We will carefully consider the review suggestions to further enhance our method and evaluation, to come up with a stronger manuscript for the next submission.

Specifically, we plan to
- Revise our manuscript to improve clarity. We will reorganize the paper and give more detailed descriptions of our designs for greater clarity.
- Have a comprehensive evaluation of our method. We will illustrate how our method benefits from the characteristics of our designs. More datasets and existing methods can be included in the comparison experiment. Method details will be analyzed with figures and tables.
